children: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is advocating less restrictive controls on overseas access to advanced U.S. artificial intelligence chips, potentially benefiting data center companies with ties to his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, The New York Times reported.

For investors, the debate could shape Nvidia’s international sales and the growth prospects of data center operators serving Chinese customers. Tighter restrictions could limit equipment purchases and computing contracts, while narrower rules could preserve those businesses but prolong regulatory uncertainty.

Washington prohibits direct sales of leading Nvidia chips to China, but Chinese companies can legally rent computing capacity at overseas facilities. Administration officials disagree over how extensively to restrict that access, with Lutnick favoring a more limited approach, according to the report.

The Commerce Department’s proposal would cover seven countries and future chip shipments, exempting equipment already installed. Certain Chinese AI training activity would require government notification without automatically triggering a licensing requirement. Other officials favor worldwide restrictions.

Cantor, now led by Lutnick’s sons, helped arrange Bitdeer stock offerings, including one of up to $1 billion this year. Bitdeer’s planned Malaysian facility is expected to generate $1.7 billion over five years and will likely serve Tencent, the Times reported, citing someone familiar with the arrangement.

The overlapping relationships raise potential conflict-of-interest concerns, although the Times found no evidence that Cantor’s business influenced Lutnick’s decisions. Commerce said he has complied with ethics agreements and does not discuss departmental matters with his sons. Lutnick transferred his remaining Cantor ownership to his family in 2025.

title: Lutnick backs narrower AI chip controls as family firm’s business draws scrutiny
